records.title: The Myth of Osiris, Isis, and the Sacred Resurrection
records.summary: A foundational epic of ancient Egyptian religion and folklore, the wise King Osiris was murdered by his jealous brother Set, who tricked him into lying inside an ornate cedar chest, sealed it with molten lead, and cast it into the Nile. Osiris's devoted sister-wife, the goddess Isis, searched across the Mediterranean to Byblos to recover his corpse. Discovering this, Set dismembered the body into fourteen pieces and scattered them across Egypt. Isis patiently searched the marshlands, gathering every fragment except the phallus (eaten by a fish), wrapping the body in sacred linen bands with the aid of Anubis to perform the first mummification. Transforming into a kite bird, she fanned life into Osiris, who became the eternal Lord of the Duat (the Underworld).
alternate_names: Isis and the Mummification of Osiris
records.historical_period: Old Kingdom to Ptolemaic Era (Pyramid Texts and Plutarch's De Iside et Osiride)
records.region_or_community: Nile River Valley, Abydos, and Philae

records.title: The Tale of the Doomed Prince (Papyrus Harris 500)
records.summary: Recorded in the New Kingdom Papyrus Harris 500, a long-awaited royal prince was born to the Pharaoh, but the Seven Hathors decreed his inescapable fate at birth: he must die by a crocodile, a snake, or a dog. To protect him, the Pharaoh built an isolated palace in the desert. Growing to manhood, the prince insisted on facing his destiny, accompanied by a loyal hound. Traveling to the kingdom of Mitanni (Naharina), he leaped seventy cubits into the air to win the hand of the Syrian princess. While he slept, his faithful wife killed a venomous viper drawn to his bed with bowls of wine, while his loyal dog chased away a giant Nile crocodile, exploring the timeless battle between human agency and divine destiny.
alternate_names: The Three Fates of the Pharaoh's Son
records.historical_period: New Kingdom (18th Dynasty, c. 13th Century BCE Papyrus Harris 500)
records.region_or_community: Thebes, Upper Egypt and Mitanni borderlands

records.title: The Tale of the Shipwrecked Sailor and the Serpent King
records.summary: Preserved in the Middle Kingdom Papyrus Leningrad 1115, an Egyptian sailor recounts his miraculous survival after a colossal storm wave shattered his ship in the Red Sea, drowning all one hundred and twenty crewmen. Washed ashore on the enchanted phantom island of the Ka, he encounters a towering divine serpent thirty cubits long with scales of gold and lapis lazuli. Fearing death, the sailor prostrates himself, but the benevolent Serpent King comforts him, recounting how his own seventy-four serpent siblings were incinerated by a falling celestial star. Showering the sailor with ivory, frankincense, myrrh, and baboons, the serpent prophesies a rescue ship's arrival, telling him the enchanted island will submerge beneath the waves forever once he departs.
alternate_names: The Serpent King of the Island of the Ka
records.historical_period: Middle Kingdom (12th Dynasty, c. 2000 BCE, Papyrus Leningrad 1115)
records.region_or_community: Red Sea and Punt trade routes, Upper Egypt

records.title: The Tale of the Two Brothers (Anpu and Bata)
records.summary: Recorded in the 19th Dynasty Papyrus D'Orbiney, elder brother Anpu and younger brother Bata live as devoted farmers. When Anpu's wife falsely accuses Bata of attempting to seduce her after Bata rejected her advances, Anpu hides behind the stable door with a spear to kill his brother. Warned by speaking cows, Bata flees, praying to the sun god Ra, who places a crocodile-infested river between them. Bata cuts off his own phallus to prove his innocence and retreats to the Valley of the Cedar, placing his heart upon the blossoming cone of a cedar tree. Through transformations into a magnificent sacred bull (Apis) and two giant persea trees, Bata outwits betrayal to become Pharaoh of Egypt.
alternate_names: The Story of the Two Brothers
records.historical_period: New Kingdom (19th Dynasty, reign of Seti II c. 1200 BCE)
records.region_or_community: Nile Delta and Valley of the Cedar (Phoenicia)

records.title: Isis and the Secret True Name of Ra
records.summary: In ancient Egyptian magical belief, true divine authority and omnipotence resided in knowledge of an entity's secret, hidden name (ren). When the supreme sun god Ra grew old, drooling upon the earth as he walked across the heavens, the great sorceress Isis gathered his divine spittle, mixed it with clay, and shaped it into a venomous viper. Placing the serpent on Ra's celestial pathway, it struck the sun god with excruciating, burning agony that none of the gods could heal. Approaching him, Isis offered to purge the poison on one condition: Ra must reveal his secret, unuttered name to her. Burning in agony, Ra whispered his secret name into Isis's breast, transferring supreme cosmic magical authority to her and her son Horus.
alternate_names: The Sorcery of the Goddess Isis
records.historical_period: New Kingdom (preserved in the Turin Papyrus of Magical Spells c. 1200 BCE)

records.title: The Legend of the Eye of Horus (Wedjat)
records.summary: During the epic eighty-year struggle between Horus and Set for the royal throne of Egypt, the fierce god of chaos Set gouged out Horus's left eye—the Eye of the Moon—and tore it into six pieces, scattering them across the desert. The ibis-headed god of wisdom, Thoth, gathered the shattered pieces, healed the wounds with his spittle, and reassembled them into the whole, magical Wedjat Eye (meaning 'The Whole/Restored One'). Each fragment corresponded to the mathematical fractional components of Egyptian measurement (1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/16, 1/32, 1/64). Horus sacrificed his restored eye by offering it to his deceased father Osiris, giving the dead god sight in the underworld and making the Eye of Horus the supreme amulet of healing and protection.
records.historical_period: Old Kingdom through Ptolemaic Era (Book of the Dead Chapter 140)
records.region_or_community: Temple of Edfu and Kom Ombo, Upper Egypt

records.title: The Eloquent Peasant and the Nine Petitions
records.summary: Preserved across four Middle Kingdom papyri, a humble peasant from the Wadi Natrun named Khun-Anup journeyed toward Herakleopolis with his donkeys laden with natron, salt, and reeds. A corrupt landowner named Nemtynakht spread a cloth across the narrow dike, and when a donkey nibbled a stalk of barley beside the path, Nemtynakht seized the peasant's beasts and goods. Seeking justice from the High Steward Rensi, the peasant delivered nine dazzling philosophical speeches on the sacred cosmic principle of Ma'at (truth, justice, and balance). Charmed by the peasant's extraordinary eloquence, Pharaoh Nebkaure ordered the petitions transcribed on papyrus scrolls, returning all stolen property to the peasant and giving him the corrupt noble's estate.
alternate_names: Khun-Anup and the Rule of Ma'at
records.region_or_community: Wadi El Natrun and Herakleopolis Magna (Beni Suef)

records.title: King Khufu and the Magicians (Westcar Papyrus)
records.summary: Recorded in the celebrated Berlin Westcar Papyrus, the great Pyramid-builder Pharaoh Khufu (Cheops) is entertained in his palace by his royal sons, who recount astonishing feats of master magicians. Prince Hardedef presents the centenarian sage Djedi of Djed-Sneferu, who eats five hundred loaves of bread and drinks one hundred jars of beer daily. Djedi demonstrates his supernatural power before the Pharaoh by decapitating a goose, placing its head on one side of the hall and its body on the other; uttering incantations, the head hops forward, the body waddles to meet it, and the bird quacks joyfully restored, before the wizard prophesies the birth of the first three kings of the Fifth Dynasty.
records.historical_period: Old Kingdom setting (4th Dynasty), compiled Middle Kingdom (Hyksos Era c. 1650 BCE)

records.title: The Myth of the Heavenly Cow and the Wrath of Sekhmet
records.summary: Preserved in royal New Kingdom tombs including Tutankhamun's shrine, the sun god Ra perceived that humanity was plotting rebellion against his elderly reign in the desert. In wrath, Ra dispatched his fiery eye in the form of the fierce lioness goddess Hathor-Sekhmet to slaughter the conspirators. Tasting human blood, Sekhmet was seized by an insatiable bloodlust, wading through humanity and threatening to exterminate the entire human race. Taking pity on mortal survivors, Ra ordered seven thousand jars of barley beer mixed with red ochre from Elephantine to resemble pools of human blood, flooding the fields. Drinking the crimson brew until she became drunk, Sekhmet fell asleep and woke as the gentle cat goddess Bastet, saving humanity from annihilation.
alternate_names: The Book of the Heavenly Cow
records.historical_period: New Kingdom (recorded in the Valley of the Kings tombs c. 1330 BCE)
community_attributions: Valley of the Kings tomb artists

records.title: The Dream Stele of Thutmose IV and the Great Sphinx
records.summary: Erected between the front paws of the Great Sphinx of Giza, the Dream Stele records an extraordinary event from the youth of Prince Thutmose (later Pharaoh Thutmose IV). While hunting wild lions in the desert sands around midday, the prince rested in the shadow of the colossal stone monument, which was buried up to its neck in shifting desert sands. In a dream vision, the sun god Harmakhis-Khepri-Re spoke from the stone mouth of the Sphinx, promising that if Thutmose cleared away the choking sand dunes and restored the sanctuary, the god would grant him the Double Crown of Upper and Lower Egypt. Honoring the divine pact, Thutmose excavated the monument and erected the red granite commemorative stele in 1401 BCE.
